title: Authentication (OIDC)
summary: OpenID Connect lets an app sign users in without ever handling their password. The browser is redirected to an identity provider, which authenticates the user and returns a one-time code. The app's backend exchanges that code for tokens, keeps them server-side, and gives the browser only an HttpOnly session cookie. APIs then verify signed access tokens without calling the identity provider.

walkthrough.title: Start login
walkthrough.text: The browser hits /login on the app backend (BFF). It generates a random state, a nonce, and a PKCE code_verifier, stores them in a short-lived pre-auth session, and redirects to the identity provider.

walkthrough.title: Authorization request
walkthrough.text: The browser follows the redirect to /authorize with client_id, redirect_uri, scope=openid, state, nonce, and code_challenge = SHA-256(code_verifier).

walkthrough.title: Authenticate the user
walkthrough.text: The identity provider checks the password against a slow hash, runs MFA such as a passkey, applies lockout rules, and starts its own single sign-on session.

walkthrough.title: Callback with a code
walkthrough.text: The identity provider redirects back to the BFF's /callback?code=…&state=…. The BFF rejects the request unless state matches what it stored in step 1.

walkthrough.title: Exchange the code
walkthrough.text: Server to server, the BFF posts the code plus code_verifier to /token and receives an id_token, a short-lived access_token, and a refresh_token. It validates the id_token's signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and nonce.

walkthrough.title: Call an API
walkthrough.text: The browser sends only its HttpOnly, SameSite session cookie. The BFF attaches the access token, and the API verifies the JWT signature locally using cached public keys (JWKS).

walkthrough.title: Refresh silently
walkthrough.text: When the access token expires, the BFF exchanges the refresh token for new tokens. Refresh tokens rotate on every use, and reuse of an old one revokes the whole session.

data.label: Browser (SPA)
responsibilities: Follows redirects between the app and the identity provider; never sees tokens in this pattern.
Sends the HttpOnly session cookie, which JavaScript (including injected XSS) cannot read.
Sends a CSRF token header on state-changing requests.

failureModes.scenario: Tokens stored in localStorage (the pattern this design avoids)
failureModes.impact: Any XSS bug can exfiltrate long-lived tokens.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep tokens server-side in the BFF; the browser holds only an opaque session ID.

failureModes.scenario: Third-party cookie blocking breaks silent renew in iframes
failureModes.mitigation: BFF refreshes server-side; no hidden-iframe renewal needed.

data.label: App Backend (BFF)

output.name: Token request
output.type: POST /token { grant_type: authorization_code, code, code_verifier, client_id } + client auth

responsibilities: Acts as a confidential OAuth client; generates state, nonce, and PKCE values and verifies them on callback.
Validates the id_token, then stores tokens in a server-side session keyed by an opaque cookie.
Proxies API calls with the access token and refreshes it before expiry.

failureModes.impact: Login CSRF: the victim is logged in to the attacker's account.
failureModes.mitigation: Reject any callback whose state doesn't match the pre-auth session; make state single-use.

failureModes.impact: Every user is logged out at once.
failureModes.mitigation: Replicated store; the IdP's SSO session lets users sign back in with one click.

data.label: Authorization Server (IdP)

output.name: Tokens
output.type: JWT id_token { iss, sub, aud, exp, nonce } + access_token + refresh_token

responsibilities: Authenticates users and maintains its own SSO session across all apps.
Issues one-time codes bound to the PKCE challenge, and only to pre-registered, exact-match redirect URIs.
Signs tokens with a private key and rotates refresh tokens, detecting reuse.

failureModes.impact: Nobody can log in; existing sessions keep working until their tokens expire.
failureModes.mitigation: Multi-region IdP; access tokens long enough to ride out short blips (5-15 min).

failureModes.scenario: Wildcard or loosely matched redirect URI
failureModes.impact: Authorization codes leak to an attacker-controlled URL.
failureModes.mitigation: Exact string matching of registered redirect URIs; PKCE makes stolen codes useless.

data.label: User Directory

output.name: Identity
output.type: JSON: { sub, email, email_verified, groups[], mfa_enrolled[] }

responsibilities: Stores password hashes using a deliberately slow algorithm (Argon2id or bcrypt) with a per-user salt.
Holds profile claims and group memberships that become token claims.
Tracks failed attempts for lockout and credential-stuffing detection.

failureModes.impact: Accounts with reused passwords are taken over.
failureModes.mitigation: Rate limits per IP and account, breached-password checks, mandatory MFA.

failureModes.scenario: Different responses for unknown users vs wrong passwords
failureModes.mitigation: Identical responses and timing for both cases.

data.label: MFA / Passkeys
responsibilities: Issues a WebAuthn challenge that the user's device signs; the signature is bound to the origin, so it is phishing-resistant.
Verifies time-based one-time codes, or sends SMS codes as a weak fallback.
Records which factors were used (amr claim) so apps can demand step-up for sensitive actions.

failureModes.impact: Users who rely on SMS can't sign in.
failureModes.mitigation: Encourage passkeys; allow backup codes; avoid SMS-only enrolment.

failureModes.impact: A tired user approves an attacker's login.
failureModes.mitigation: Number matching, rate limits on prompts, or phishing-resistant passkeys instead of push.

data.label: Resource API
responsibilities: Verifies the JWT signature with the public key matching its kid header, entirely offline.
Checks iss, aud (this API), exp/nbf with small clock-skew tolerance, and required scopes.
Authorizes per resource (does this sub own this record?), not just 'is logged in'.

failureModes.scenario: Accepting alg: none or the wrong algorithm
failureModes.mitigation: Pin allowed algorithms (e.g. RS256) in the verifier; never read alg from the token.

failureModes.scenario: Revoked user still has a valid access token
failureModes.impact: Access continues until the token expires.
failureModes.mitigation: Short token lifetimes; token introspection or a deny-list for high-risk actions.

data.label: Signing Keys & JWKS

output.name: Public keys
output.type: JSON: { keys: [{ kid, kty: "RSA", alg: "RS256", n, e }] }

responsibilities: Keeps private signing keys in KMS or an HSM; the IdP signs through the KMS API, never holding raw key material.
Publishes public keys by kid so any service can verify tokens independently.
Rotates keys on a schedule, publishing the new key before using it and keeping the old one until tokens expire.

failureModes.impact: Every API rejects valid tokens at once.
failureModes.mitigation: Publish the next key in JWKS days early; refetch JWKS on unknown kid (rate-limited).

failureModes.impact: Attackers mint tokens for any user.
failureModes.mitigation: HSM-backed keys, emergency rotation runbook, and short token lifetimes to limit exposure.
